1 Executive Summary As	the	popularity	and	social	significance	of	online	gaming	have	surged,	with	 more	than	three	billion	gamers	encompassing	a	broad	spectrum	of	the	global	 population,	the	urgency	to	understand	how	gaming	spaces	constitute	formative	 identity-	and	community-building	environments	is	more	essential	than	ever.	 While	acknowledging	that	many	gamers	have	positive	experiences,	this	project	 aims	to	understand,	through	a	gender	and	intersectional	lens,	how	socialisation	 processes	coupled	with	exposure	to	harassment,	hate-based	discrimination	and	 extreme	content	can	potentially	lower	resilience	to	radicalisation	in	gaming	and	 gaming-adjacent	spaces. Governments	 are	 increasingly	 paying	 attention	 to	 this	 issue,	 considering	 regulatory	 requirements	 and	 effective	 intervention	 designs.	 This	 heightened	 awareness	necessitates	a	deeper	analysis	of	the	nuances	and	complexities	of	the	 threats	and	risks.	Therefore,	this	report	aims	to	provide	much-needed	analysis	 of	 these	 issues,	 guiding	 the	 reader	 through	 the	 key	 research	 findings	 of	 the	 project	‘Examining	Socialization	with	a	Nexus	to	Radicalization	Across	Gaming	 (-Adjacent)	 Platforms	 Through	 a	 Gender	 Lens’,	 which	 was	 funded	 by	 Public	 Safety	Canada,	led	by	RUSI	and	implemented	by	a	consortium	of	members	of	 the	Extremism	and	Gaming	Research	Network. Taking	a	cross-cultural	global	approach	and	drawing	on	primary	survey	data	 and	data	collected	from	and	on	multiple	gaming	and	gaming-adjacent	platforms,	 this	project	aims	to	provide	accessible	gender-sensitive	research	analysis,	along	 with	pragmatic	recommendations	for	practitioners	and	policymakers	engaged	 in	these	spaces.	Following	a		conceptual	framing	section	and	a	chapter	outlining	 project	scope	and	methodology,	project	analysis	highlights	the	following	four	 key	analytical	focuses: 1.	 An	assessment	of	the	prevalence	of	harmful,	toxic	and	extremist	content	in	 gaming	spaces. 2.	 Identification	 of	 the	 importance	 of	 (offline)	 identity	 and	 culture	 in	 the	 formation	of	gamer	identity	and	communities. 3.	 Analysis	of	gender	norms	and	dynamics	in	gaming	communities	and	their	 potential	exploitation	for	radicalisation	and	recruitment. 4.	 Exploration	 of	 where	 gendered	 socialisation	 processes	 combined	 with	 normalised	exposure	to	extreme	ideas	and	content	can	reduce	resilience	to	 radicalisation. Overall,	this	project	adds	new	insights	to	the	growing	body	of	research	on	the	 topic	of	extremism	and	gaming	through	the	gender	and	intersectional	lens	it

I n	an	era	when	digital	interactions	shape	our	daily	lives,	the	intersection	of	 gaming	and	radicalisation	has	emerged	as	a	critical	concern.	Online	gaming	 platforms,	once	seen	exclusively	as	venues	for	entertainment	and	socialisation,	 are	now	recognised	as	spaces	where	extremist	ideologies	can	flourish.	With	an	 estimated	3.2	billion	people	playing	video	games	globally, 1	encompassing	a	broad	 spectrum	of	the	global	population,	the	urgency	to	understand	how	these	spaces	 can	 become	 breeding	 grounds	 for	 radicalisation	 has	 never	 been	 greater.	 Governments	 are	 increasingly	 paying	 attention	 to	 this	 issue	 and	 considering	 regulatory	requirements;	companies	are	deliberating	trust	and	safety	policies;	 and	parents,	guardians	and	teachers	are	concerned	about	child	welfare.	This	 heightened	 awareness	 necessitates	 a	 deeper	 analysis	 of	 the	 nuances	 and	 complexities	of	these	threats	and	risks.	 This	report	aims	to	provide	much-needed	analysis	of	these	issues,	guiding	the	 reader	through	the	key	research	findings	and	analysis	of	the	project	‘Examining	 Socialization	with	a	Nexus	to	Radicalization	Across	Gaming	(-Adjacent)	Platforms	 Through	a	Gender	Lens’,	which	is	funded	by	Public	Safety	Canada,	led	by	RUSI	 and	implemented	by	a	consortium	of	members	of	the	Extremism	and	Gaming	 Research	Network.2	The	project	aims	to	understand,	through	a	Gender-based	 Analysis	Plus	(GBA+)	model, 3	how	socialisation	processes	coupled	with	exposure	 to	extreme	content	can	potentially	lower	resilience	to	radicalisation	on	gaming	 and	 gaming-adjacent	 platforms. 4	 Specifically,	 it	 investigates	 whether	 these	 processes	 are	 formed	 around	 specific	 in-group	 identities	 or	 the	 othering	 of	 out-groups,	and	how	they	are	influenced	by	the	digital	and	transnational	nature

Through	survey	and	data	analysis,	the	research	aims	to	contribute	 to	the	discourse	on	extremism	in	these	spaces	by	identifying	dynamics	in	gaming	 environments	 that	 might	 contribute	 to	 increased	 vulnerability	 to	 extremist	 beliefs.	By	considering	gender	and	other	intersectional	identity	factors	such	as	 age,	religion,	race,	etc.,	the	GBA+	model	allows	for	a	comprehensive	analysis	of	 how	misogyny	and	other	forms	of	identity-based	discrimination	may	reduce	 resilience	to	radicalisation	and	facilitate	the	spread	of	extremism	across	different	 cultural	and	geographical	contexts	within	gaming	environments.	GBA+	further	 allows	 for	 this	 report’s	 findings	 and	 recommendations	 to	 support	 efforts	 to	 develop	more	responsive	and	inclusive	policies,	programmes	and	other	initiatives,	 by	accounting	for	gender-	and	diversity-sensitive	factors	from	the	analytical	to	 the	response	stages. The	research	takes	a	cross-cultural	global	approach,	drawing	on	primary	data	 from	Canada,	the	US,	the	UK,	Germany,	France,	Australia	and	Indonesia.	The	 project	 aims	 to	 provide	 accessible	 research	 analysis,	 along	 with	 pragmatic	 recommendations	for	practitioners	and	policymakers,	to	enhance	knowledge	 and	programme	effectiveness	in	addressing	these	pressing	issues.	By	understanding	 the	 types	 of	 content	 and	 community	 dynamics	 that	 are	 most	 impactful,	 the	 findings	 in	 this	 report	 aim	 to	 inform	 counter-radicalisation	 efforts	 and	 the	 development	of	inclusive	and	safe	gaming	communities. This	report	begins	with	a	chapter	outlining	the	project,	its	research	objectives	 and	 the	 methodology,	 including	 the	 research	 design	 and	 tools	 used	 for	 data	 collection	 and	 analysis.	 The	 core	 of	 the	 report	 and	 project	 analysis	 is	 then	 presented	in	four	subsequent	chapters.	Chapter	II	examines	key	findings	on	the	 prevalence	of	extremist,	toxic	and	harassing	content	across	gaming	and	gaming- adjacent	platforms.	Chapter	III	explores	the	formation	of	gamer	identities	and	 how	these	intersect	with	offline	identities.	Chapter	IV	analyses	how	gendered	 behaviours	and	expectations	influence	interactions	and	susceptibility	to	extremist	 content	within	gaming	communities.	Chapter	V	considers	how	the	dynamics	of	 identity,	socialisation	and	exposure	converge	to	create	potential	pathways	for	 radicalisation	in	these	spaces. Context The	gaming	industry	has	experienced	an	unprecedented	boom	in	popularity	in	 recent	years,	‘with	revenue	on	track	to	top	US$300	billion	in	2028	–	more	than	 double	its	level	in	2019’. 9	This	growth	is	accompanied	by	a	significant	increase	 in	 the	 diversity	 of	 the	 online	 gaming	 environment.	 The	 gaming	 market	 has	 expanded	to	include	mobile,	console,	in-browser	and	PC	games,	along	with	a	 variety	 of	 gaming	 environments	 such	 as	 esports,	 publications,	 forums	 and	 gaming-adjacent	 platforms,	 and	 the	 growth	 of	 gaming	 cultural	 references.	 Gaming-adjacent	 platforms	 –	 spaces	 that	 support	 and	 enhance	 the	 gaming	 experience	but	are	not	games	themselves	–	include	platforms	such	as	Discord	 (forums/messaging),	 Steam	 (forums/messaging	 and	 game	 market),	 Twitch	 (livestreaming)	 and	 DLive	 (livestreaming).	 These	 platforms	 are	 essential	 for	 understanding	today’s	online	gaming	landscape,	as	they	provide	spaces	where	 gamers	 interact,	 share	 content	 and	 form	 communities	 beyond	 the	 gameplay	 itself. 10	 As	the	popularity	and	social	significance	of	online	gaming	have	surged,	so	too	 has	concern	about	its	exploitation	by	terrorist	entities.	Events	such	as	the	gamified	 terror	 attack	 in	 Christchurch,	 New	 Zealand,	 on	 15	 March	 2019,	 highlighted	 potential	links	between	gaming	and	violent	extremism,	making	this	an	emerging	 area	of	both	concern	and	research. This	research	includes,	but	is	 not	limited	to,	examining	gamified	acts	of	terrorism,	investigating	how	gaming	 spaces	might	facilitate	radicalisation,	and	examining	broader,	often	interconnected,	 risks	associated	with	toxicity	in	gaming	culture,	such	as	hate-based	discrimination,	 harassment,	sexism	and	racism. 11 Over	the	past	five	years,	a	series	of	studies	has	mapped	out	the	primary	ways	 extremists	exploit	gaming	spaces,	identifying	six	key	methods:	 1.	 Creating	bespoke	games	and	modifications	(‘mods’)	of	existing	games.	 2.	 Using	 gamification	 (the	 use	 of	 design	 elements	 of	 games	 in	 non-gaming	 contexts)	for	radicalisation.	 3.	 In-game	communication.	 4.	 Incorporating	gaming	cultural	references	into	propaganda.	 5.	 Exploiting	gaming-adjacent	spaces.	 6.	 Using	gaming	for	financing	and	money-laundering	purposes. 12	 Emerging	research	has	also	explored	the	social	and	identity	dynamics	within	 gaming,	revealing	vulnerabilities	to	radicalisation.	For	instance,	‘identity	fusion’	 with	gaming	culture	–	where	an	individual	forms	a	deep,	visceral	alignment	 with	their	social	group,	in	this	case,	gamers	–	has	been	shown	to	uniquely	predict	 in	certain	communities	antisocial	attitudes	and	negative	outcomes,	including	 racism,	sexism	and	potential	endorsement	of	extreme	ideas	and	behaviours. 13	 Conceptual	Framework While	existing	research	has	documented	the	strategic	and	organic	use	of	gaming	 spaces	 by	 extremist	 actors,	 there	 is	 still	 only	 limited	 understanding	 of	 how	 exposure	to	extremist	or	other	harmful	content	in	these	spaces	impacts	individual	 and	community	susceptibility	to	radicalisation. 7 Radicalisation through Gaming: The Role of Gendered Social Identity Jessica White et al. exposure	often	involves	hate,	discrimination,	harassment	and	toxic	behaviour,	 frequently	 manifesting	 as	 gender-	 and	 other	 identity	 factor-based	 hate	 and	 harassment.	 Research	 shows	 that	 hate,	 discrimination	 and	 harassment	 are	 rife	 in	 online	 gaming	spaces.	A	2023	report	indicated	that	in	the	US,	approximately	83	million	 out	of	110	million	online	gamers	were	exposed	to	hate	and	harassment	while	 playing	video	games	in	that	year	alone. 14	Studies	indicate	that	repeated	exposure	 to	hate-based	narratives	and	participation	in	communities	that	reinforce	divisive	 in-group/out-group	dynamics	may	shape	individuals’	attitudes	towards	extremism. 15	 This	research	extends	its	focus	to	these	types	of	exposure	to	hate	and	harassment,	 in	addition	to	exposure	to	specific	extremist	ideologies.	In	doing	so,	it	recognises	 that,	 while	 more	 research	 is	 needed	 to	 understand	 the	 connections	 with	 radicalisation	or	recruitment	into	violent	extremist	groups	or	ideologies,	such	 exposure	can	shape	community	norms	and	potentially	make	individuals	more	 vulnerable	to	extremist	ideologies.	This	is	particularly	relevant	for	individuals	 immersed	in	communities	that	encourage	such	attitudes,	as	these	environments	 can	effectively	socialise	members	into	a	mindset	conducive	to	extremist	views. Definitions Extremism and violent extremism: In	the	context	of	this	study,	‘extremism’	is	 understood	as	the	advocacy	of	ideologies	or	practices	that	oppose	democratic	 values,	social	inclusivity	and	equal	rights,	often	involving	hate-based,	exclusionary	 or	discriminatory	narratives. 22	For	the	purposes	of	this	report,	‘violent	extremism’	 goes	further,	by	endorsing	or	inciting	violence	to	advance	ideologies,	crossing	 the	line	from	harmful	belief	systems	into	actions	that	result	in	or	support	offline	 harm.23	 The	 distinction	 is	 important,	 as	 not	 all	 extremism	 involves	 explicit	 violence,	although	the	two	can	be	closely	linked,	with	extremist	ideologies	often	 providing	fertile	ground	for	radicalisation	into	violent	extremism. Given	that	gaming	spaces	are	transnational	in	nature,	defining	extremism	and	 violent	extremism	is	challenging,	due	to	the	differing	legal	standards	and	cultural	 interpretations	 that	 exist	 across	 countries.	 For	 example,	 content	 labelled	 as	 extremist	 in	 one	 jurisdiction	 may	 be	 deemed	 permissible	 in	 another.	 This	 ambiguity	 is	 further	 compounded	 by	 individual	 perceptions,	 as	 there	 is	 no	 universal	standard	for	what	constitutes	extremism.	Recognising	this	complexity,	 this	research	aimed	to	capture	exposure	to	a	range	of	content	types	that	reflect	 varying	levels	of	extremism,	from	explicit	calls	to	violence	to	subtler	exclusionary	 narratives	that	can	foster	extremist	attitudes. 60 Conclusion T he	research	presented	in	this	Whitehall	Report	highlights	that	gaming	 spaces	are	dynamic	and	highly	diverse	ecosystems,	varying	significantly	 across	countries,	platforms	and	types	of	games.	In	the	same	way,	individuals	 active	in	gaming	spaces	are	far	from	monolithic;	they	vary	vastly	by	cultural,	 national	and	individual	identity,	each	of	which	impacts	their	vulnerability	and	 resilience	to	hate-based	discrimination	and	extremism	in	different	ways.	To	take	 an	 example,	 while	 gamers	 in	 the	 US	 and	 Indonesia	 report	 high	 levels	 of	 identification	 with	 their	 gamer	 identities	 and	 higher	 exposure	 to	 extremist	 content,	Canadian	gamers	are	less	likely	to	experience	exclusion	based	on	identity	 factors	than	gamers	in	other	countries.	 The	research	demonstrates	that	hate	and	harassment	are	pervasive	in	gaming	 spaces,	yet	their	manifestations	and	impacts	vary,	especially	along	gender	lines.	 Female	 and	 LGBTQI+	 gamers	 consistently	 report	 higher	 rates	 of	 exclusion,	 harassment	and	misogynistic	targeting,	indicating	an	intersectional	experience	 that	impacts	exposure	to	harmful	narratives.	While	identity-based	harassment	 is	a	global	issue	in	gaming,	countries	such	as	the	US,	Australia	and	Germany	 report	 some	 of	 the	 highest	 rates	 of	 identity-based	 exclusion,	 revealing	 areas	 where	 community	 management	 and	 regulatory	 intervention	 might	 be	 more	 focused	to	build	safer	online	environments. The	 intersection	 of	 online	 gaming	 culture	 and	 offline	 identities	 and	 cultural	 norms	can	create	fertile	ground	for	the	reinforcement	of	toxic	behaviours	and	 the	propagation	of	extremist	ideologies	in	gaming	spaces.	The	normalisation	of	 toxicity,	harassment	and	extremism,	coupled	with	the	reinforcement	of	gendered	 stereotypes	in	gaming	spaces,	indicates	a	pressing	need	for	interventions	that	 address	these	harmful	dynamics.	The	findings	of	this	project	also	emphasise	 the	 importance	 of	 considering	 gender	 and	 other	 intersecting	 identities	 in	 understanding	how	radicalisation	can	take	root	in	gaming	spaces,	as	well	as	 how	it	spreads.	This	includes	a	need	to	better	understand	how	gendered	ideology	 is	wielded	in	gaming	spaces,	as	well	as	how	shared	gender	narratives	can	help	 to	connect	and	spread	extremist	ideologies	in	these	spaces.	A	closer	examination	 of	these	interactions	is	critical,	as	it	reveals	how	extremist	narratives	may	exploit	 or	reinforce	societal	inequities,	making	gender-sensitive	and	culturally	informed	 interventions	essential. This	report	has	opened	new	pathways	for	understanding	the	complex	relationships	 between	gaming,	identity	and	radicalisation.	However,	it	has	also	highlighted	 the	need	for	further	research	to	fully	grasp	how	these	dynamics	play	out	across
